questions.question: The bus pass rises from R500 to R575 and monthly passengers fall from 2 000 to 1 880. Calculate the price elasticity of demand, state the sign convention, and classify the demand.
questions.expected_answer: Price change: 75/500 x 100 = 15% increase. Quantity change: 120/2000 x 100 = 6% decrease. Elasticity = 6%/15% = 0,4 (strictly −0,4; the negative sign reflects the inverse price-quantity relationship and we interpret the absolute value). Since 0,4 is below one, demand is inelastic — passengers barely respond to the fare increase.

questions.question: Name and explain three determinants of price elasticity of demand, each with a South African example in a because-sentence.
questions.expected_answer: Any three of: availability of substitutes — one brand of instant noodles is elastic because five rivals share the shelf, while a chronic medicine with no generic is inelastic; necessity versus luxury — maize meal is inelastic because households must eat, while a professional car wash is elastic because a bucket at home does the job; share of income — candles are inelastic because they claim cents, while school transport is more elastic because a ten percent rise moves real money; time — electricity is inelastic in the month of a tariff hike but more elastic after two years because households fit timers, LED bulbs and solar panels; habit — cigarettes are inelastic because addiction blocks the way out, which is why the duties on them collect reliably.

questions.question: Using the car-wash numbers (price R60 to R75, weekly washes 240 to 144), show what happens to total revenue and state the full three-line rulebook linking elasticity and revenue.
questions.expected_answer: Before: R60 x 240 = R14 400. After: R75 x 144 = R10 800 — revenue fell R3 600 because demand is elastic (1,6). Rulebook: with inelastic demand, price and total revenue travel in the same direction, so a price rise grows revenue; with elastic demand they travel in opposite directions, so a price cut grows revenue; at unitary elasticity small price changes leave revenue untouched — revenue is at its summit. Caution: revenue is not profit, since extra sales carry extra costs.
